headline: The Every Student Succeeds Act reauthorizes and rewrites federal K-12 education law, shifting school accountability and testing rules from federal control toward states.
what_it_does: This law amends the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and reauthorizes many K-12 programs through fiscal year 2020. It replaces the old Adequate Yearly Progress system with state-designed accountability systems that use multiple indicators, including graduation rates and school growth measures. It also lets states set their own academic standards and long-term goals, limits federal control over curriculum, and consolidates many smaller grant programs into larger formula grants.

who_it_affects.group: Public elementary and secondary school students, especially low-income students and English learners
who_it_affects.how: Their schools must be rated under new state accountability systems, and schools with consistently underperforming groups must create targeted improvement plans.
States must write new state plans, set their own standards and goals, identify lowest-performing schools, and publish annual report cards.
Districts must follow revised poverty-based funding rules, parent involvement requirements, and improvement plan rules for identified schools.

who_it_affects.group: Students in juvenile justice or foster care systems
who_it_affects.how: States must help them re-enroll in school and offer credit-bearing coursework, and the definition of at-risk now covers students with prior child welfare contact.
The federal highly qualified teacher requirement is replaced by state certification and licensure rules, and states must report on teacher effectiveness criteria.

who_it_affects.group: Parents and families of public school students
who_it_affects.how: Districts must notify parents about assessment policies, teacher qualification requests, and English learner services, and outreach now includes extended family members.
States may use alternative academic standards and alternative assessments for them, with extra oversight if more than 1 percent of an district's students take them.
A new competitive grant program funds opening and expanding high-quality charter schools, and states may receive more than one facilities aid grant.

who_it_affects.group: Impact Aid districts near federal lands or bases
who_it_affects.how: Payment formulas, eligibility rules, and property valuation methods were changed, and the Coast Guard was added to the definition of Armed Forces.
The Education for Homeless Children and Youths program was reauthorized, and the definition now excludes children awaiting foster care placement.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 10, 2015; most provisions apply to school years beginning after that date, with some phase-ins and programs authorized through fiscal year 2020.
